{{Short description|Theoretical relationship in oceanography}}
The '''Sverdrup balance''', or '''Sverdrup relation''', is a theoretical relationship between the [[wind stress]] exerted on the surface of the open [[ocean]] and the vertically integrated [[meridional]] (north-south) transport of ocean water.

== History ==

Aside from the oscillatory motions associated with [[tide|tidal]] flow, there are two primary causes of large scale flow in the ocean: ''(1)'' [[thermohaline]] processes, which induce motion by introducing changes at the surface in [[temperature]] and [[salinity]], and therefore in [[seawater density]], and ''(2)'' wind forcing.  In the 1940s, when [[Harald Sverdrup (oceanographer)|Harald Sverdrup]] was thinking about the physical processes determining the gross features of [[ocean current|ocean circulation]], he chose to focus on the wind stress component of the forcing.  As he says in his 1947 paper,<ref name="Sverdrup1947">{{Cite journal |last=Sverdrup |first=H. U. |date=1947 |title=Wind-Driven Currents in a Baroclinic Ocean; with Application to the Equatorial Currents of the Eastern Pacific |url=https://pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.33.11.318 |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=33 |issue=11 |pages=318–326 |doi=10.1073/pnas.33.11.318 |issn=0027-8424}}</ref> in which he presented the Sverdrup relation, this is probably the more important of the two.  

Sverdrup was motivated by what had been a long-standing mystery of ocean circulation: While most of the major ocean surface currents flow downwind, the equatorial Atlantic and Pacific Oceans both feature a strong and persistent [[Equatorial Counter Current]] that flows east against the prevailing trade winds, a few degrees north of the equator. He wrote “Our specific problem is to determine whether the equatorial currents, including the counter currents, can be accounted for on the basis of our knowledge of the wind stress only".<ref name="Sverdrup1947" />

== Derivation ==

Sverdrup made simplifying assumptions by neglecting friction (except that of the wind stress on the ocean surface), time variability (thus the balance represents the mean state), and the advective (nonlinear) terms of the [[Navier-Stokes equations]], and by considering only the top-to-bottom vertically integrated currents in a flat-bottomed ocean.<ref name="Sverdrup1947" /> These are consequential restrictions that remove - in addition to thermohaline influences - many factors affecting ocean circulation, including mixing, boundary currents, and the ability to portray the vertical structure, but nevertheless reproduce in broad strokes the large-scale features of the currents.

With Sverdrup's simplifying assumptions, the resulting [[barotropic]] momentum equations become

<math>
\begin{aligned}
-f V &= -P_x + {\tau^x} \\
f U &= -P_y + {\tau^y} 
\end{aligned}
</math>

with the continuity equation

<math> U_x + V_y = 0 </math> ,

where upper-case variables are vertically integrated, <math  display=inline>f</math> is the [[Coriolis parameter]], <math  display=inline>U</math> and <math  display=inline>V</math> are the eastward and northward transport components (in units of m<sup>2</sup>/s), <math  display=inline>P</math> is the (integrated) pressure, <math display=inline>\tau</math> is the wind stress (direction indicated by superscripts <math display=inline>x,y</math>), subscripts indicate derivatives. For simplicity of notation, both <math  display=inline>P</math> and <math display=inline>\tau</math> are understood to be divided by the background density of seawater <math display=inline>\rho_0</math>, thus the units of <math  display=inline>P_{x,y}</math> and <math  display=inline>\tau</math> are m<sup>2</sup>/s<sup>2</sup>. Sverdrup's top-to-bottom vertical integration in steady state leads to the simplified (non-divergent) continuity equation.

The simplified momentum equations can be expressed as sums of the well-known [[geostrophic current|geostrophic]] and [[Ekman transport|Ekman]] flow types:  <math display=inline>(U,V)=(U,V)_{geostrophic}+(U,V)_{Ekman}</math>. 

Sverdrup’s analysis proceeded with the crucial first step of taking the [[Curl (mathematics)|Curl]] of the momentum equations (<math  display=inline>\partial/\partial y </math> of the first minus <math  display=inline> \partial/\partial x </math> of the second), using <math  display=inline>\beta = \partial f /\partial y</math> to define the variation of the Coriolis parameter with latitude (<math  display=inline>\beta</math> is approximated as a constant). Then use continuity to remove the <math  display=inline>(U_x+V_y)</math> term. 

The result is the Sverdrup balance defining the meridional transport entirely in terms of the wind: <math> \beta V = Curl(\tau)</math> .

Continuity then gives the corresponding zonal transport:

<math>U_x = -V_y = -\frac{1}{\beta} \frac{\partial}{\partial y} Curl(\tau) \Longrightarrow U = -\frac{1}{\beta} \int_{x_e}^x \frac{\partial}{\partial y} Curl(\tau) dx </math> ,

where <math  display=inline>x_e</math> is the eastern boundary of the ocean.

Since the vertically-integrated fluid is horizontally non-divergent, a [[streamfunction]] <math  display=inline>\psi</math> exists:

<math>\psi = \frac{1}{\beta} \int_{x_e}^x Curl(\tau) dx</math> , where <math>V =  \psi_x</math>  , <math>U =  -\psi_y</math> , <math>\psi(x_e) = 0 </math>.

Because flow is along streamfunction contours, it is a convenient way to display the resulting circulation (first figure below).

==Interpretation==

Taking the Curl of the momentum equations in this way has several advantages:
* In practical terms it removes the pressure gradient terms. These require ocean observations that are hard to measure accurately or sample adequately.
* The balance has <math  display=inline>\beta</math> but no <math  display=inline>f</math>, thus continuous solutions are available across the equator.
* Unlike the momentum equations, the Sverdrupian expression for <math display=inline>\psi</math> produces a clear and simple eastern boundary condition: <math>\psi(x=x_e)=0</math> expresses the obvious fact that there can be no flow through the eastern boundary, so the coast is a streamline. Integrating the curl westward from the coast depicts a circulation derived from the wind alone.
* A vorticity equation describes what the wind does to the ocean on the large scale: stretching and squashing a column of water and thereby changing its spin.

The last of these is an example of conservation of [[potential vorticity]] in Rossby’s shallow water formulation,<ref name="Rossby1939" /> in which the local and planetary rotations balance in steady state. A parcel at rest with respect to the surface of the earth must match the spin of the earth underneath it. Looking down on the earth at the north pole, this planetary spin is counterclockwise, which is defined as positive rotation or vorticity. At the south pole it is clockwise, corresponding to negative rotation. Thus, for example, to move a parcel of fluid northward without causing it to gain local spin, it must acquire sufficient (positive) rotation so as to keep it matched with the rotation of the earth underneath it. The left-hand side of the Sverdrup equation represents the meridional motion required to maintain this match between the absolute vorticity of a water column and the planetary vorticity, while the right represents the applied rotational force of the wind.

==Illustrations of the Sverdrup Circulation in the North Pacific==

[[File:ERS winds and Sverdrup streamfunction for Eikipedia.png|thumb|Top: ERS (scatterometer) winds; bottom Sverdrup_streamfunction. These figures are expanded views of fields used to show the circulation west of Central America<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2002 |title=Mean Three-Dimensional Circulation in the Northeast Tropical Pacific* |url=http://journals.ametsoc.org/doi/10.1175/1520-0485(2002)0322.0.CO;2 |journal=Journal of Physical Oceanography |volume=32 |issue=9 |pages=2457–2471 |doi=10.1175/1520-0485(2002)032<2457:MTDCIT>2.0.CO;2 |issn=0022-3670|doi-access=free }}</ref>. ]]
[[File:Sverdrup and Argo U for Eikipedia.001.png|thumb|Zonal currents in the N Pacific: (top) Sverdrup U from wind only, (bottom) Observed geostrophic U from [[Argo (oceanography)|Argo profiling floats]].]]

Sverdrup made his calculation of the wind, curl and zonal current using the very limited observational data available at that time<ref name="Sverdrup1947" />. These illustrations show examples of the calculations described above from modern satellite wind stress (vectors; scale at top left) and its curl (shading, in units of 10<sup>&minus;7</sup>N&nbsp;m<sup>&minus;3</sup>, top panel) from the [[European Remote-Sensing Satellite]] ERS-1 and 2 [[Scatterometer|Scatterometers]] on a 1 degree grid, averaged over 1991-2000, distributed by [[EUMETSAT]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=EUMETSAT - User Portal |url=https://user.eumetsat.int/catalogue/EO:EUM:DAT:ERS:OSI-152 |access-date=2026-07-28 |website=user.eumetsat.int |doi=10.15770/EUM_SAF_OSI_0009}}</ref>. These winds, their curl, and the resulting Sverdrup streamfunction are frequently used to illustrate the circulation<ref name="KC2013" /><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Kessler |first=William S. |last2=Johnson |first2=Gregory C. |last3=Moore |first3=Dennis W. |date=2003 |title=Sverdrup and Nonlinear Dynamics of the Pacific Equatorial Currents* |url=http://journals.ametsoc.org/doi/10.1175/1520-0485(2003)0332.0.CO;2 |journal=Journal of Physical Oceanography |language=en |volume=33 |issue=5 |pages=994–1008 |doi=10.1175/1520-0485(2003)033<0994:SANDOT>2.0.CO;2 |issn=0022-3670}}</ref><ref name="Qiu2009" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Brown |first=Jaclyn N. |last2=Godfrey |first2=J. Stuart |last3=Schiller |first3=Andreas |date=2007-05-01 |title=A Discussion of Flow Pathways in the Central and Eastern Equatorial Pacific |url=http://journals.ametsoc.org/doi/10.1175/JPO3042.1 |journal=Journal of Physical Oceanography |language=en |volume=37 |issue=5 |pages=1321–1339 |doi=10.1175/JPO3042.1 |issn=1520-0485}}</ref>. Most of the curl is due to <math display="inline">\partial \tau^x / \partial y</math>. The blue shading of the subtropical gyre (north of about 15°N) reflects negative rotation due to the change from westerly (from the west) winds in mid-latitudes to easterly trade winds in the subtropics. The region of positive curl (red) along about 7°N is where easterly winds decrease towards the equator; this feature of the wind produces the North Equatorial Counter Current (NECC) that was Sverdrup’s target. The resulting Sverdrup streamfunction in the bottom panel shows the circulation produced by this wind pattern: Flow is along streamfunction contours (emphasized by overlaid gray arrows, with the NECC labeled).

The lower figure compares the zonal currents represented by the Sverdrup streamfunction shown above to observed currents: orange indicates eastward flow, blue westward. The top panel is calculated from the wind alone via the Sverdrup balance; eastward flow (orange) along the north edge, and westward across the central gyre (blue), are shown<ref name=":0" />. The NECC is the orange band along 5°-10°N. The bottom panel shows observed geostrophic currents calculated from ocean observations ([[Argo float]] density); which has a similar pattern, indicating that the Sverdrup balance captures these features<ref name=":0" />. The Sverdrupian representation is smoother than the observed currents but has the same structure and magnitude (but see [[#Weaknesses of the Sverdrup formulation|Weaknesses]] below), in particular showing the eastward NECC flowing east against the wind and convincingly explaining the longstanding mystery that motivated Sverdrup.

==Weaknesses of the Sverdrup formulation==
The Sverdrup circulation is repeatedly found to be a robust representation of the vertically-integrated steady ocean transports away from the coastlines of low and mid-latitude oceans.<ref name="Chavanne">{{Cite journal |last=Chavanne |first=Cédric |last2=Flament |first2=Pierre |last3=Lumpkin |first3=Rick |last4=Dousset |first4=Bénédicte |last5=Bentamy |first5=Abderrahim |date=2002 |title=Scatterometer observations of wind variations induced by oceanic islands: Implications for wind-driven ocean circulation |url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.5589/m02-047 |journal=Canadian Journal of Remote Sensing |language=en |volume=28 |issue=3 |pages=466–474 |doi=10.5589/m02-047 |issn=0703-8992|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Qiu2009"> {{Cite journal |last=Qiu |first=Bo |last2=Chen |first2=Shuiming |last3=Kessler |first3=William S. |date=2009-02-01 |title=Source of the 70-Day Mesoscale Eddy Variability in the Coral Sea and the North Fiji Basin* |url=http://journals.ametsoc.org/doi/10.1175/2008JPO3988.1 |journal=Journal of Physical Oceanography |language=en |volume=39 |issue=2 |pages=404–420 |doi=10.1175/2008JPO3988.1 |issn=1520-0485}}</ref><ref name="KC2013">{{Cite journal |last=Kessler |first=William S. |last2=Cravatte |first2=Sophie |date=2013 |title=Mean circulation of the Coral Sea |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/2013JC009117 |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Oceans |language=en |volume=118 |issue=12 |pages=6385–6410 |doi=10.1002/2013JC009117 |issn=2169-9291}}</ref><ref name="KHD2019">{{Cite journal |last=Kessler |first=William S. |last2=Hristova |first2=Hristina G. |last3=Davis |first3=Russ E. |date=2019-07-01 |title=Equatorward western boundary transport from the South Pacific: Glider observations, dynamics and consequences |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0079661118303021 |journal=Progress in Oceanography |volume=175 |pages=208–225 |doi=10.1016/j.pocean.2019.04.005 |issn=0079-6611|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="K2002">{{Cite journal |date=2002 |title=Mean Three-Dimensional Circulation in the Northeast Tropical Pacific* |url=http://journals.ametsoc.org/doi/10.1175/1520-0485(2002)0322.0.CO;2 |journal=Journal of Physical Oceanography |volume=32 |issue=9 |pages=2457–2471 |doi=10.1175/1520-0485(2002)032<2457:MTDCIT>2.0.CO;2 |issn=0022-3670|doi-access=free }}</ref> Weaknesses of this approach are found most prominently in the [[Southern Ocean]], where the lack of a meridional barrier precludes integration from a known eastern boundary condition. 
The narrow, intense [[western boundary currents]] are explicitly excluded by the neglect of friction in the Sverdrup formulation, so the westward integration that defines the streamfunction is valid only east of a narrow western boundary layer. These strong currents fundamentally depend on friction of some kind, either with the bottom (in Stommel’s simple calculation<ref name="Stommel1948" />), or with the western coastline (Munk,<ref name="Munk1950" /> Godfrey<ref name="Godfrey" />). (See [[#Further Developments|Further Developments]] below). Physically, this dependence occurs because the integration of wind curl forcing can accumulate vorticity that grows to the west (e.g., anti-cyclonic vorticity in the subtropical gyres) that must be dissipated to allow a closed circulation. 

Regions where strong eddy activity is important to the dynamics are similarly out of its scope; these include the Southern Ocean, the exit regions where the western boundary currents turn offshore 
<ref name="Ducet2000">Ducet, N., Le Traon, P.Y. and G. Reverdin, 2000. Global high-resolution mapping of ocean circulation from TOPEX/Poseidon and ERS-1 and -2. J. Geophys. Res. (O, 105(C8) 19477-19498. https://doi.org/10.1029/2000JC900063</ref> 
(note the large magnitude mismatch between Sverdrup and observed currents along 35°N east of Japan where the [[Kuroshio Current]] leaves the coast; see [[#Examples of the Sverdrup Circulation in the North Pacific|Examples]] above), and eddies in several regions produced by shear between adjacent horizontal currents.<ref name="Qiu2009" /> Sverdrup's simplifying choice to restrict attention to the vertically-integrated circulation means that the balance cannot describe details of vertical flows, for example the [[upwelling]] commonly found along the west coasts of North and South America, or equatorial upwelling.

==Further developments==

In 1948 [[Henry Stommel]] proposed a way around the inability to describe western boundary currents in the Sverdrup formulation, starting with the same equations as Sverdrup but adding bottom friction.<ref name="Stommel1948">{{Cite journal |last=Stommel |first=Henry |date=1948 |title=The westward intensification of wind-driven ocean currents |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1029/TR029i002p00202 |journal=Eos, Transactions American Geophysical Union |language=en |volume=29 |issue=2 |pages=202–206 |doi=10.1029/TR029i002p00202 |issn=2324-9250|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This showed that the variation in the [[Coriolis effect|Coriolis parameter]] with latitude results in a narrow [[western boundary current]] in [[ocean basin]]s. In 1950, [[Walter Munk]] combined the results of [[Carl-Gustaf Rossby|Rossby]] (eddy viscosity 
<ref name="Rossby1939">Rossby, C. G.; Collaborators (1939). "Relation between variations in the intensity of the zonal circulation of the atmosphere and the displacements of the semi-permanent centers of action". Journal of Marine Research. 2 (1): 38–55. https://doi/10.1357/002224039806649023. S2CID 27148455.</ref>
), Sverdrup (upper ocean wind driven flow), and Stommel (western boundary current flow), and proposed a complete solution for the ocean circulation.<ref name="Munk1950">{{Cite journal |last=Munk |first=Walter H. |date=1950 |title=ON THE WIND-DRIVEN OCEAN CIRCULATION |url=http://journals.ametsoc.org/doi/10.1175/1520-0469(1950)0072.0.CO;2 |journal=Journal of Meteorology |language=en |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=80–93 |doi=10.1175/1520-0469(1950)007<0080:OTWDOC>2.0.CO;2 |issn=0095-9634|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

There remained the problem of islands, since none of these solutions explained how the westward integration could be restarted if interrupted by an island. This is a particularly important problem due to the position of [[Australia]] between the Pacific and [[Indian Ocean]]s, and meant that no Sverdrupian solution for the Indian Ocean circulation was available. In 1989, roughly 40 years after the earlier studies, Stuart Godfrey of [[CSIRO Marine and Atmospheric Research]] developed a methodology of comparable simplicity known as the “[[The Godfrey Island Rule|Island Rule]]” 
<ref name="Godfrey">{{Cite journal |last=Godfrey |first=J. S. |date=1989 |title=A sverdrup model of the depth-integrated flow for the world ocean allowing for island circulations |url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/03091928908208894 |journal=Geophysical & Astrophysical Fluid Dynamics |language=en |volume=45 |issue=1-2 |pages=89–112 |doi=10.1080/03091928908208894 |issn=0309-1929|url-access=subscription }}</ref> 
to explain how the effects of a Sverdrup circulation to the east could be communicated to the west side of the “island”, and the westward integration could be continued. This enabled the Sverdrup streamfunction to be extended across the Indian Ocean, connecting the wind-driven circulation across both basins in what has been called the "Southern Hemisphere Super Gyre".<ref name="Quetal2018">Qu, T., I.Fukumori and R.A. Fine, 2018. Spin-up of the Southern Hemisphere Super Gyre. J. Geophys. Res. (O), 124(1), 154-170. https://doi.org/10.1029/2018JC014391</ref> 
Other significant islands where the Godfrey method is needed include [[Madagascar]] and several of the larger and mountainous South Pacific islands ([[New Zealand]], [[Fiji]], [[Vanuatu]], [[New Caledonia]] and the [[Solomon Island]] chain <ref name="KHD2019" />).
